title: Do Quantum Models Scale Like LLMs?
authors: David S. Berman, Ying-Jer Kao, Roger G. Melko, Alexander G. Stapleton
abstract: In this work, we study the neural scaling laws of RydbergGPT, an autoregressive transformer model trained on qubit projective measurement data gathered from interacting Rydberg atom arrays. The quantum system is known to exhibit a finite-size remnant of a critical point as the laser detuning parameter is varied. We find that near the critical point the transformer loss as a function of training dataset size is well described by a power-law with a loss floor correction. However, away from criticality the quality of the power-law description is substantially reduced. We then compare the statistical structure of both Rydberg measurements and natural-language corpora using an entropy-normalised, finite sample corrected mutual information "two-point" function. We find that near-critical statistics of the two point functions are closest to those observed in natural-language, whilst other qubit configurations far from the critical point have two-point functions that decay more rapidly. This supports the hypothesis that multi-scale dependence contributes to stable neural scaling, and that scaling behaviour should be viewed as a property of the model-data pair.
summary: This work tests the hypothesis that quantum systems near a critical point exhibit scaling laws analogous to those seen in LLMs. By training a transformer on Rydberg atom measurements, the authors found that stable power-law scaling occurs only near criticality. Furthermore, the statistical dependencies of these near-critical quantum measurements closely match those found in natural language, suggesting multi-scale structure is key to robust scaling.
main_problem: To investigate whether the scaling laws observed in Large Language Models (LLMs) are replicated when training transformers on quantum measurement data from interacting Rydberg atoms.
main_result: The transformer loss exhibits stable power-law scaling near the quantum critical point, and the statistical structure of these near-critical measurements most closely resembles that of natural language corpora.
method: The study uses autoregressive transformers (RydbergGPT) to model qubit projective measurements and compares the resulting statistical dependencies using entropy-normalized mutual information 'two-point' functions.
model_or_system: The physical system is an interacting Rydberg atom array modeled by a Hamiltonian involving interaction terms and controlled by a laser detuning parameter ($\delta$). The model is trained on the resulting qubit projective measurement data.
key_observables: Transformer loss vs. dataset size, and the entropy-normalized, finite sample corrected mutual information 'two-point' function $	ext{b}I(r)$.
important_parameters: The laser detuning parameter ($\delta$), especially near the critical point ($\delta/\Omega \approx 1.1$), and the effective dataset size ($D_{	ext{eff}}$).
main_assumptions: The scaling behavior is hypothesized to be a property of the model-data pair, and the analysis relies on fitting empirical power-law ansatze to both loss and mutual information.
figures_summary: Figures show representative occupation-basis measurements, data-scaling curves for the loss near and far from criticality, and mutual information profiles comparing Rydberg measurements to natural language corpora.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the quantum model and its critical behavior. It then analyzes the loss scaling laws, showing power-law behavior near criticality. Finally, it compares the statistical structure via mutual information, finding the strongest analogy to language near the critical point.
why_interesting: It bridges the gap between machine learning scaling laws and fundamental physics, suggesting that critical phenomena might manifest as universal scaling behaviors in information-theoretic measures, which is highly relevant for understanding complex quantum many-body systems.
